shape.name: Receptive Skills — Reading
shape.description: A reading lesson built around a current-affairs article on electric vehicles, with a listening main task and a structured discussion finale.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Reading is taught through explicit question-type strategies before the task, then applied first to a shared reading and then to a listening read-along. A differentiated B2 challenge text allows fast finishers to extend. The lesson closes with an opinion-reason-evidence discussion so reading feeds directly into speaking.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end, students will [read + discuss with evidence].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Receptive Skills — Reading
Are EV cars the wave of the future?

stages.stage: Lead-in: What do you know about electric cars?
stages.stage_aim: Activate prior knowledge about electric cars.
procedure: Show the splash slide (EV cars charging). Ask: "What do you see? What might this lesson be about?" Let students speculate freely.
Advance to the title slide: "Are EV cars the wave of the future?" Confirm the theme.
Open-class discussion: "Why do people buy electric cars? Are they cheaper to run?" Accept all answers; do not correct yet.

stages.stage_aim: Pre-teach four words that block comprehension of the text.
procedure: Show the red transition "Let's check your word knowledge".
Present each word with the 3-click reveal: phonemic script, then the word, then a context sentence.
Words: wasteful, junkyard, outlive, plugged in. Do NOT teach "convinces" — it is tested in Question 5.

stages.stage_aim: Introduce the question types in the reading and how to answer them.
procedure: Detail questions (Q1, Q2, Q7): find the exact fact; scan for key words.
Main idea and author's purpose (Q3, Q4): read the first sentence of each paragraph.
Vocabulary in context (Q5): guess the meaning from the surrounding clues.
Inference and attitude (Q6, Q8): read between the lines.
After each strategy, complete the "Try it" demo table on the slideshow.

stages.stage_aim: Read the B1 text together and answer the eight questions.
procedure: Read the B1 article aloud together, paragraph by paragraph (text is on the worksheet).
Students answer the eight multiple-choice questions.
Challenge for fast finishers: "Grab a B2 text from the back of the room and see if you can complete it with 10 minutes to go."

stages.stage_aim: Listen to the narrated text while following along, then self-check answers.
procedure: Play the monolog audio: the narrator reads the B1 text aloud.
Students follow along on the worksheet and complete or confirm their answers.
Gallery walk: students walk around and check their answers against the pre-printed answer posters on the walls.

stages.stage_aim: Give a structured opinion using evidence from the text.
procedure: Show the O-R-E structure: Opinion, Reason, Evidence (yellow label under the opening question).
Drill the interaction language: I agree with you because... / I see your point, but... / So we both think...
Topic: "Should everyone switch to electric cars?" Students give an opinion, a reason, and evidence from the text.
Run the 8-minute timer.

metadata.topic: Are EV cars the wave of the future?
materials: B1 reading: "Why your opinion of used electric vehicles is probably wrong" (adapted from New Scientist, 22 April 2026) — article + 8 multiple-choice questions
B2 challenge reading: "The Quiet Revolution: One in Five New Cars Is Now Electric" (adapted from IEA Global EV Outlook 2025)
Slideshow: Are EV cars the wave of the future? (30 slides)
Worksheet: B1 questions (and B2 challenge questions)
Pre-printed B1 and B2 answer posters for the gallery walk
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, students will be able to read and understand an article about electric cars, identify common reading question types, and give a structured opinion using evidence from the text.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Students will practise listening while reading and use language of agreement and disagreement in discussion.
answer_key: 1. D — Car parts should wear out with the car. Henry Ford thought it was wasteful for any part to last longer than the car itself.
2. A — Buyers think the battery will give out early. This fear makes used electric cars lose value faster than petrol or diesel cars.
3. C — The author wants to correct a wrong idea about used EVs. He shows that batteries can last longer than the cars, so used EVs are a better deal than most people think.
4. D — Battery life makes used electric cars a good buy. Well-looked-after batteries can last longer than the cars themselves.
5. C — "Convinces" means makes people decide to do something. Money, not the climate, is what finally convinces people to go electric.
6. B — Slower sales are probably not the end of EV success. The writer ends on a hopeful note: the future for electric cars seems more certain.
7. A — Making money from battery storage may attract more buyers. Owners can get paid for storing electricity for the national energy system.
8. B — The writer is confident that EVs will succeed. Cheaper batteries, cheaper charging, and battery income all point to a more certain future.
